column2: Also on the authority of Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) that some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the Prophet ﷺ:

“The people of wealth have gone off with the rewards: they pray as we pray, they fast as we fast, and they give in charity from the surplus of their wealth.” He said: “Has Allah not given you things with which to give charity?

Every tasbīḥah (saying subḥān Allāh) is a charity, every takbīrah (saying Allāhu akbar) is a charity, every taḥmīdah (saying al-ḥamdu lillāh) is a charity, every tahlīlah (saying lā ilāha illā Allāh) is a charity, enjoining good is a charity, forbidding evil is a charity, and in the intimate relations of one of you there is a charity.” They said: “O Messenger of Allah,
does one of us fulfil his desire and have a reward for it?”
He said: “Do you not see that if he were to put it in something unlawful, he would bear a sin for it?
Likewise, if he puts it in what is lawful, he has a reward.” Reported by Muslim.
The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were the most eager of people for every good and the quickest to every good, competing in righteous deeds,

and each would love to catch up in reward with those of them who were ahead. That is why a group of the poor among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned that the rich shared with them in prayer and fasting,

while being distinguished above them by giving charity from the surplus of their wealth. The Prophet ﷺ showed them that there are kinds of charity the poor are able to give, such as words of remembrance, enjoining good and forbidding evil.
The charities that the Prophet ﷺ guided the poor to do are of two kinds:

a kind whose benefit is confined to them, namely saying subḥān Allāh, Allāhu akbar, al-ḥamdu lillāh and lā ilāha illā Allāh; and a kind that extends beyond them to others, benefiting them and others, namely enjoining good, forbidding evil and marital relations.

Permissible things that a person does for the soul's own enjoyment become acts of devotion through a righteous intention, such as fulfilling his desire when he intends by it to keep himself and his wife chaste and to have children.
The Companions were eager to do righteous deeds and competed in good deeds.
Charity is not limited to giving wealth in charity, even though that is its basic form.
The hadith encourages saying subḥān Allāh, Allāhu akbar, al-ḥamdu lillāh and lā ilāha illā Allāh, and shows that this is a charity from the Muslim to himself.
Whoever is unable to do some act of obedience because he lacks the means to it should do many of the acts of obedience he is able to do.
The hadith encourages enjoining good and forbidding evil, and shows that this is a charity from the Muslim to himself and to others.
A person's fulfilling his desire with a righteous intention is a charity from him to himself and to others.
One may question a scholar about what he has said in order to be sure of it.

The hadith affirms analogy (qiyās), because the Prophet ﷺ likened the reward of one who fulfils his desire lawfully to the sin incurred by one who fulfils it unlawfully; the analogy in this hadith is of the kind called inverse analogy (qiyās al-ʿaks).
